issues.legal_issue: A belated challenge to an industrial plant’s location does not, by itself, require cancellation of its licence or closure when the location was disclosed and the plant proceeded with official permissions.
material_facts: The company disclosed the proposed site in its licence application, and the Central Government issued an industrial licence after processing the application.
State authorities granted permissions for construction and operation, and the plant had operated for years.
The distance-based location objection was raised for the first time before the Supreme Court and was not seriously argued there.
issues.conclusion: The location objection did not justify cancellation of the licence or closure of the plant at that stage. The Central and State Governments could still consider whether the plant should be shifted to a site satisfying the applicable location conditions.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 11 of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951, the Central Government may impose location conditions; the use of “may” makes that power directory. Issuing a licence after the proposed location was disclosed could amount to waiving the location requirements for that unit. The Court also relied on the late raising of a factual location objection after permissions and prolonged operation.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_operating_industrial_plant and licence_application_disclosed_site and licence_issued_after_site_disclosure and state_permissions_granted and location_objection_raised_late

predicates.appeal_challenges_operating_industrial_p: The proceeding challenges the licence or continued operation of an industrial plant.
predicates.licence_application_disclosed_site: The operator stated the proposed site in its application for an industrial licence.
predicates.licence_issued_after_site_disclosure: The licensing authority issued the licence after receiving an application that disclosed the proposed site.
predicates.state_permissions_granted: State authorities granted permissions for construction or operation at the proposed site.
predicates.location_objection_raised_late: The challenger raised the location objection only after the plant had received permissions and begun operating.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an operating plant, its site was disclosed in the licensing process, permissions were granted, and the location objection was raised late, the objection alone does not require cancellation or closure.

issues.legal_issue: An environmental consent prescribing pollution limits below binding standards must be corrected and complied with, but closure need not be ordered in the first instance.
material_facts: The Pollution Control Board’s consent prescribed limits below those required by the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986.
Tests indicated that the plant’s effluent exceeded the prescribed environmental standards.
The plant had installed pollution-control equipment, operated with consent for years, and had not been the subject of a serious argument that it had in fact violated the statutory standards.
issues.conclusion: The Pollution Control Board had to correct its consent to conform to the applicable standards and require the plant to comply. If the plant failed to comply with the corrected consent and standards, the authorities could direct closure.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 3 and Schedule I, Entry 50-B of the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986 permit State Boards to prescribe higher standards, not lower ones. The Court treated compliance with those binding standards as necessary while declining immediate closure in light of the permissions, investment in pollution controls, and operating history.

predicates.appeal_challenges_environmental_consent_: The proceeding challenges environmental consent for a plant that is operating.
predicates.consent_limits_below_binding_environment: The consent sets pollution limits less stringent than the standards binding on the regulator.
predicates.plant_has_pollution_controls_and_operati: The plant installed pollution-control equipment and operated for a substantial period under regulatory consent.

issues.definition: When an operating plant’s consent sets limits below binding standards and the plant has pollution controls and an operating history, the consent must be corrected and compliance enforced before closure is considered.

issues.legal_issue: The public has no right under the Water Act to demand information from a Pollution Control Board before it issues a consent.
material_facts: A third party claimed a right to obtain analysts’ reports and submit objections before the Pollution Control Board issued its consent.
The challenge alleged that withholding the reports violated the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression.
issues.conclusion: The consent was not invalid because the reports had not been disclosed to the third party before its issuance; Section 25 of the Water Act did not confer the asserted pre-consent information right.
issues.legal_principle: The Court interpreted Section 25 of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, in the context of Sections 16, 17 and 20, and concluded that it did not give members of the public a right to demand information before consent was issued.

predicates.appeal_challenges_pollution_consent_for_: The proceeding challenges a pollution consent on the ground that information was not disclosed.
predicates.third_party_demands_information_before_c: A person other than the operator seeks reports or other information before the regulator issues consent.

issues.definition: When a third party challenges pollution consent because reports were not supplied before consent, that nondisclosure does not invalidate the consent.

issues.legal_issue: A defect in a Pollution Control Board’s composition does not invalidate its consent merely because the defect existed when the consent was issued.
material_facts: The Board’s chairperson and member secretary did not possess the qualifications required for those positions.
The challenge to the consent relied on that defect in the Board’s composition.
issues.conclusion: The defect did not invalidate the consent because the Water Act provided that a Board’s acts or proceedings could not be questioned merely for a vacancy or defect in its constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4(2)(a) and 4(2)(f) of the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 specify qualifications for the chairperson and member secretary. Section 11 provides that a Board’s act or proceeding is not to be called in question merely because of a vacancy or defect in its constitution.

predicates.appeal_challenges_pollution_consent_for_: The proceeding challenges pollution consent because of a defect in the regulator’s composition.
predicates.board_officers_lacked_required_qualifica: The regulator’s chairperson or member secretary lacked the qualifications required for the office.
predicates.composition_defect_is_the_basis_of_chall: The asserted basis for invalidating the regulator’s act is the defect in its composition.

issues.definition: When a consent is challenged solely because the regulator’s officers lacked required qualifications, the consent is not invalidated merely by that composition defect.

issues.legal_issue: An abattoir’s operation cannot be treated as causing livestock depletion when regional data and expert assessments do not establish a sustained decline, and courts ordinarily do not re-evaluate technical findings absent a sufficient basis to do so.
material_facts: The Court considered reports from government expert committees and livestock census figures covering periods before and after the abattoir began operating.
The reports and census figures did not show a steep or persistent decline in buffalo numbers in the relevant region; the figures instead showed increases in several periods and areas.
Officials were assigned to monitor slaughter and conduct animal examinations under the applicable State law.
The appellants challenged the reliability and method of the expert reports and census figures, but the Court found no basis to conclude that the expert bodies’ findings were perverse or arbitrary.
issues.conclusion: The Court found no reason to conclude that the abattoir’s operation depleted the buffalo population and rejected that ground for stopping its operation.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 6(1) and 6(2) of the Andhra Pradesh Prohibition of Cow Slaughter and Animal Preservation Act, 1977 require a certificate for slaughter and prohibit slaughter of animals likely to remain useful for breeding, milking or draught purposes. The Court relied on Systopic Laboratories (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Dr. Prem Gupta & Ors. and K. Vasudevan Nair & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors. for the principle that courts ordinarily do not interfere with findings of expert bodies on technical and scientific matters. It also considered regional, multi-year data more probative of trends than figures for a single year.

predicates.appeal_challenges_abattoir_on_livestock_: The proceeding challenges an abattoir’s operation on the ground that it depletes livestock.
predicates.expert_reports_and_regional_multiyear_da: Expert assessments and data covering the relevant surrounding region and multiple years do not show a sustained livestock decline attributable to the operation.
predicates.no_perversity_or_arbitrariness_shown_in_: The challenger does not establish that the technical findings are perverse or arbitrary.

issues.definition: When an abattoir is challenged for livestock depletion but regional multi-year evidence shows no sustained decline and the expert findings are not shown to be perverse or arbitrary, the abattoir is not stopped on that ground.

issues.legal_issue: A meat-export policy that permits export subject to certification that the animals were not used for breeding or milking is not unconstitutional merely because it may affect livestock, and it remains subject to government review.
material_facts: The challenged policy encouraged the export of meat and permitted export of buffalo meat subject to certification that the animals were not used for breeding or milking.
The Court found no depletion of buffalo wealth attributable to the abattoir’s operation and no serious or grave error by the governments in adopting the policy.

The Court recognized that the policy could have potentially harmful effects on livestock and directed the Central Government to review it in light of those effects and the constitutional Directive Principles.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to strike down the meat-export policy and directed the Central Government to review it in light of the Directive Principles and its potential effects on livestock and the economy.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 19(1)(g), 21, 39(b) and (c), 47, 48, 48-A and 51-A(g) were considered. The Court relied on Mohd. Hanif Quareshi & Ors. v. State of Bihar and State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat & Ors., holding that Directive Principles and fundamental duties inform review of restrictions but do not, by themselves, invalidate a policy. It also relied on the Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority Act, 1985, Section 2(i) and Schedule item 2, concerning the Authority’s role in promoting export and development of scheduled products.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_meat_export_: The proceeding asks the court to invalidate a government policy encouraging meat exports on constitutional grounds.
predicates.policy_allows_export_subject_to_nonprodu: The policy allows export only with certification that the animals were not used for breeding or milking.
predicates.no_serious_or_grave_governmental_error_s: The challenger does not establish a serious or grave error in the government’s adoption of the policy.

issues.definition: When a meat-export policy requires certification that animals were not used for breeding or milking and no serious governmental error is shown, the policy is not invalidated but remains subject to review.

issues.legal_issue: A prosecution for a litigant’s alleged misstatement need not proceed when the Court finds no reason to continue it in the circumstances of the appeal.
material_facts: A High Court had directed prosecution of a litigant for an alleged misstatement about an earlier proceeding seeking similar relief.
The Supreme Court had stayed operation of that direction while the appeals were pending.
After disposing of the appeals, the Supreme Court found no reason to proceed with the prosecution.
issues.conclusion: The Court directed that the prosecution should not proceed further.
issues.legal_principle: The Court exercised its authority in disposing of the appeals and considered the effect of its interim stay and the circumstances of the proposed prosecution under Section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, read with Section 191 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.

predicates.appeal_challenges_direction_to_prosecute: The proceeding includes a challenge to an order directing prosecution of a litigant.
predicates.prosecution_direction_was_stayed: The prosecution direction was stayed while the appeal was pending.
predicates.court_finds_no_reason_to_continue: On considering the matter, the court finds no reason for the prosecution to continue.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a stayed prosecution direction and the court finds no reason to continue the prosecution, it does not proceed.

issues.legal_issue: State authorities must strictly implement existing statutory animal-protection duties and maintain institutions for the care and protection of cattle where the statute requires them.
material_facts: Public-interest petitions sought enforcement of existing statutory protections for cattle and establishment of institutions to care for animals.
The High Court had stated that the Government and its officers were required to enforce the statutory provisions, although it dismissed the petitions.
The Supreme Court directed strict enforcement and implementation and required proper institutions for cattle care and protection.
issues.conclusion: The appeals were allowed in part, with directions to the State Government and its authorities to strictly enforce the relevant statutory provisions and maintain proper institutions for cattle care and protection.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4, 8 to 11 and 18 of the Mysore Prevention of Cow Slaughter and Cattle Preservation Act, 1964 impose statutory requirements concerning slaughter, enforcement and institutions for animal care. The Court held that statutory provisions must be strictly complied with by the responsible State authorities.

predicates.public_interest_proceeding_seeks_enforce: The proceeding seeks enforcement of existing legal protections for animals and provision for their care.
predicates.statute_imposes_enforcement_and_care_dut: The applicable law assigns the State duties concerning enforcement and institutions for animal care.
predicates.high_court_recognized_state_duty_but_dis: The lower court recognized that the State had an enforcement duty but nevertheless dismissed the proceeding.

issues.definition: When a public-interest proceeding seeks enforcement of existing animal protections, the law imposes enforcement and care duties, and the lower court recognized but did not give effect to those duties, the State must perform them.

issues.legal_issue: A restriction on a fundamental right that advances a Directive Principle may be reasonable if it does not clearly conflict with the right and is within the enacting legislature’s competence.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the relationship between Directive Principles and fundamental rights had to be reconsidered in light of later constitutional decisions.

The Court applied a Constitution Bench decision that had overruled the earlier approach on this point and described the conditions under which a restriction aimed at securing Directive Principles could be upheld.
issues.conclusion: The Court decided this constitutional issue in favour of the appellants, holding that a restriction aimed at securing Directive Principles may be reasonable subject to the stated limitations.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat & Ors., which overruled on this point the approach in Mohd. Hanif Quareshi & Ors. v. State of Bihar. It also relied on Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala. A restriction aimed at securing Directive Principles must not clearly conflict with the fundamental right and must be within the legislature’s competence.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge_to_restriction and restriction_advances_directive_principle and restriction_within_legislative_competence and no_clear_conflict_with_fundamental_right

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge_to_res: The proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of a restriction on a fundamental right.
predicates.restriction_advances_directive_principle: The restriction is aimed at securing a constitutional Directive Principle.
predicates.restriction_within_legislative_competenc: The legislature that enacted the restriction had authority to enact it.
predicates.no_clear_conflict_with_fundamental_right: The restriction does not clearly conflict with the fundamental right it limits.

issues.definition: A restriction challenged on constitutional grounds may be upheld as reasonable when it advances a Directive Principle, falls within legislative competence and does not clearly conflict with the affected fundamental right.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional protection for milch and draught cattle includes animals that were formerly capable of those functions but have ceased to be capable of them.
material_facts: The appellants sought a broader interpretation of the constitutional direction concerning preservation and improvement of cattle.

The Court applied the Constitution Bench’s interpretation that the relevant classification describes a species of cattle and does not exclude animals that cease to function as milch or draught cattle because of age or disability.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that the protection extends to cattle that were formerly milch or draught cattle but have ceased to be functional for those purposes.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat & Ors., which overruled the narrower interpretation in Mohd. Hanif Quareshi & Ors. v. State of Bihar. The expression “milch or draught cattle” in Article 48 describes a class that includes animals that cease to be functional through age or disability.

predicates.constitutional_interpretation_concerns_c: The proceeding requires interpretation of a constitutional direction concerning preservation of cattle.
predicates.cattle_were_formerly_milch_or_draught: The animals belonged to the class of cattle capable of providing milk or draught work during their lives.
predicates.cattle_later_ceased_to_be_functional: The animals later ceased to perform those functions because of age or disability.

issues.definition: When constitutional interpretation concerns cattle preservation and the cattle were formerly milch or draught animals that later ceased to be functional, the constitutional protection includes them.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot invalidate a partial slaughter prohibition or impose a total prohibition that the legislature did not enact, because doing so would amount to judicial legislation.
material_facts: The petitioners challenged a statutory provision that permitted slaughter of certain bovine animals subject to conditions and sought a court order imposing a total ban.
The statute did not impose a total prohibition on slaughter of all bovine cattle.
The Court observed that the Constitution Bench decision upholding a total prohibition in another statutory scheme had not held that permitting some slaughter was itself unconstitutional.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the request to declare the statutory provision unconstitutional or direct a total prohibition, holding that such relief would be judicial legislation and would encroach on legislative powers.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Kassab Jamat & Ors., which upheld a total prohibition enacted by a legislature but did not hold that laws permitting some slaughter were unconstitutional. A court cannot use a writ to create a prohibition that the legislature has not enacted.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_seeks_total_sla: The proceeding challenges the constitutionality of a slaughter law and asks the court to prohibit all slaughter.
predicates.existing_law_allows_some_slaughter: The existing law permits some slaughter subject to conditions or limitations.
predicates.legislature_has_not_enacted_total_ban: The legislature has not enacted a total prohibition on the activity.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge seeks a total slaughter ban, the existing law permits some slaughter and the legislature has not enacted a total ban, the court does not create one by judicial order.
